title: Hundreds of ships stranded in the Gulf. The legal disputes are just getting started
summary: Strait of Hormuz disruption is exposing businesses to mounting losses and legal disputes over force majeure, stranded vessels and fertilizer trade. Learn more.
body_markdown:
Disruption in the Strait of Hormuz reaches far beyond the vessels passing through it. When a critical shipping route is interrupted, the effects spread rapidly through energy markets, supply chains and commercial contracts. Deliveries may be delayed or cancelled, prices may change sharply, force majeure notices may follow and insurance coverage may be tested. For businesses trading across borders, geopolitical risk can quickly become legal risk.


The strait connects Middle East Gulf producers and international markets, making disruption significant for energy, petrochemicals, fertilizers and other traded goods. A delay at sea can affect supply obligations, financing arrangements, downstream production and the ability of counterparties to perform. This will generate disputes now and for years to come.


## Supply chains under pressure


Energy markets provide a clear starting point. Oil and liquefied natural gas shipments depend on maritime access, while petrochemicals and nitrogen fertilizers rely on many of the same inputs. Interruptions to production or shipping can therefore affect several industries at once, even where the immediate disruption occurs far from the eventual buyer.


The effects then cascade through the supply chain. Production costs rise, prices respond, downstream buyers adjust and consumer prices can come under pressure. At each stage, contractual obligations are tested against circumstances that may bear little resemblance to those assumed when the agreements were negotiated. The question then is: who pays?


Fertilizer illustrates this dynamic clearly. An August 2026 analysis by the Opec Fund estimated the closure put roughly a third of global seaborne fertilizer trade at risk and blocked around 21m tons of annual Middle East Gulf urea export capacity. Urea prices roughly doubled in April, but World Trade Organization data shows that prices had fallen substantially by June and remain far below their peak. Any sudden spike has material consequences for supply contracts where, for example, questions of efficient breach might arise.


The legal consequences reach across upstream gas supply agreements, production and offtake contracts, shipping arrangements, charterparties, cargo insurance and downstream sales.


## Force majeure and contractual disputes


The current conflict has already prompted a series of force majeure declarations by major energy and commodities producers. QatarEnergy declared force majeure on affected long-term LNG contracts with counterparties in Belgium, China, Italy and South Korea, and has since extended it repeatedly, most recently to the end of December 2026. Kuwait Petroleum Corporation and Bahrain’s Bapco Energies followed with similar declarations, while Iraq declared force majeure across all foreign-operated oilfields.


These announcements are likely only the first stage in what could become a substantial volume of commercial arbitrations.


Claims will turn on familiar but fact-intensive questions: Was a delivery failure genuinely caused by the disruption or by commercial choices made around it? Was termination permitted? How do price-adjustment clauses drafted for ordinary volatility apply to an extraordinary event? What steps were required to mitigate the impact? Under many force majeure clauses, increased cost alone will not excuse performance; the distinction between impossibility and commercial unattractiveness may be decisive. Force majeure clauses are also relatively untested before the courts, leading to uncertainty about any clause’s proper construction and whether it was validly or invalidly triggered.


Cross-border disputes can also raise difficult questions about where a counterparty holds assets and whether any eventual judgment or award can be enforced.


## Shipping, insurance and wider commercial disputes


The scale of the shipping disruption is striking. In June 2026, Allianz estimated that around 1,150 cargo-carrying vessels, representing approximately $125bn in combined vessel and cargo value, were in the Middle East Gulf awaiting a resumption of operations. Hundreds of ships remain stranded. Insurance costs also rose sharply: in July, Marsh reported additional war risk premiums of 7.5%–10% of hull value for some strait transits, translating to millions of dollars in extra insurance costs per trip. The result is a potential mix of coverage disputes, charterparty claims and commercial arbitrations, sometimes arising from the same voyage.


A single interruption may generate several overlapping disputes. Shipowners and charterers may disagree over delay, deviation, safe port obligations or the allocation of additional costs. Cargo interests may face losses from late delivery or deterioration, while insurers and insureds may dispute the scope of war risk and other coverage. These claims may involve the same shipments and events but different parties, legal regimes and fora. Trade disputes may follow as governments turn to tariffs, anti-dumping investigations and countervailing duties, while sustained cost pressure can push weaker counterparties toward insolvency, making recoverability a question to address early.


## How legal finance can help


Pursuing a major commercial claim is often expensive and slow. An arbitration over a lost cargo or a cancelled supply contract can take years and cost millions before anything is recovered, and those costs fall on businesses whose cashflow the disruption has already been squeezed.[Legal finance is designed to solve that problem](https://www.burfordcapital.com/introduction-to-legal-finance/?utm_source=ref&utm_medium=sponsored_content&utm_campaign=lloyds_list) .


Put simply, legal finance is capital provided against the value of a legal claim. A legal finance provider, such as Burford Capital, pays some or all of the fees and costs of litigation or arbitration and, in return, receives a share of any recovery. The financing is non-recourse: If the claim does not succeed, the business owes nothing, so the finance provider rather than the claimant bears the downside risk.


Legal finance can take several forms beyond single-case funding. Portfolio arrangements spread capital across a group of claims, often at a lower cost than funding each matter individually. Claim monetization advances cash against the expected value of a pending claim or award, converting a future recovery into immediate liquidity that can be used for any business purpose. Financiers can also support enforcement, financing the work of locating and recovering assets once an award or judgment has been obtained — particularly relevant where counterparties are state-owned or hold assets across multiple jurisdictions.


For businesses dealing with supply chain disruption, the appeal is practical; legal finance allows them to pursue meritorious claims without diverting operating capital at a time when cashflow may already be under strain.


## What businesses should do now


Businesses affected by force majeure ** declarations, terminations or disputed price adjustments should assess claims early: quantify the loss, evaluate the merits and consider the counterparty’s ability to pay. Where counterparties are state-owned or based overseas, enforcement should shape the claim from the outset rather than being addressed only once an award is in hand.


The recent Strait of Hormuz disruption shows how quickly a geopolitical shock can become a legal one. Businesses across globally connected industries should expect the same pattern: disruption first, disputes close behind. Businesses should prepare early; even if a matter is ultimately resolved without litigation or arbitration, geopolitical circumstances can shift with little warning, and the steps taken today may prove decisive if a dispute arises tomorrow.
